title: Recursion
summary: Methods that call themselves - base cases and recursive cases, how the call stack works, tracing factorial and Fibonacci, recursion on arrays and strings, the cost of naive recursion and memoization, StackOverflowError, and when to prefer a loop.

cards.q: What two parts does every recursive method need?
cards.a:
A base case, and a recursive case that moves toward it

The base case stops the recursion; the recursive case calls the method on a smaller problem so the base case is eventually reached. Without that, the calls pile up until `StackOverflowError`.

cards.q: Why is the plain recursive Fibonacci slow?
cards.a:
It recomputes the same smaller values again and again

`fib(n)` calls `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, which compute the same smaller values again and again, so the number of calls grows exponentially (roughly 1.6ⁿ). Memoization stores each answer once.

cards.q: What does `f(3)` print for `static void f(int n) { if (n == 0) return; f(n - 1); System.out.print(n); }`?
cards.a:
123

The print happens after the recursive call returns, so the deepest call (n = 1) prints first; `f(0)` returns without printing.
